# Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source

Srikanth Raj Chetupalli    Thippur V. Sreenivas Affiliation: Dept. of
ECE, Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore, 560012.

###### Abstract

Dereverberation of a moving speech source in the presence of other
directional interferers, is a harder problem than that of stationary
source and interference cancellation. We explore joint multi channel
linear prediction (MCLP) and relative transfer function (RTF)
formulation in a stochastic framework and maximum likelihood estimation.
We found that the combination of spatial filtering with distortion-less
response constraint, and time-varying complex Gaussian model for the
desired source signal at a reference microphone does provide better
signal estimation. For a stationary source, we consider batch
estimation, and obtain an iterative solution. Extending to a moving
source, we formulate a linear time-varying dynamic system model for the
MCLP coefficients and RTF based online adaptive spatial filter. For the
case of tracking a desired source in the presence of interfering
sources, the same formulation is used by specifying the RTF. Simulated
experimental results show that the proposed scheme provides better
spatial selectivity and dereverberation than the traditional methods,
for both stationary and dynamic sources even in the presence of
interfering sources.

###### Index Terms: 

Dereverberation, Multi channel linear prediction, Spatial filtering,
Linear dynamical system, Relative transfer function.

## I Introduction

For tele-communication, the natural speech inside an enclosure is
adversely affected by reverberation due to multiple reflections of the
source signal by the walls and other rigid surfaces in the enclosure.
This affects hands-free telephony and other man-machine interaction
tasks such as HuBot (Human-Robot) interaction, assisted hearing devices
and voice assistants relying on distant speech recognition
\[[1](#bib.bib1), [2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3), [4](#bib.bib4),
[5](#bib.bib5), [6](#bib.bib6), [7](#bib.bib7)\]. Enhancement of
reverberant speech is a challenging problem due to the long impulse
response of enclosure ($`0.5-1~s`$ typically) and the time varying
nature of speech signal properties. The problem is further compounded in
the presence of ambient acoustic or recording noise, or interfering
sources, and also a dynamic scenario where the source may be moving
changing its position over time. In this paper, we consider enhancement
of reverberant speech of a static or dynamic source, and also the
desired source signal selection in the presence of other directional
interferers.

In spatial filtering methods such as beamforming, the acoustic
propagation between the source and the microphone positions is described
using an acoustic transfer function (ATF) or ratio transfer function
(RTF) \[[8](#bib.bib8)\] and the late reverb component is treated as
noise \[[9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10)\]. The spatial selective
filtering is essential for the suppression of directional interferers
and the estimation of source from a desired spatial direction. However,
since the diffuse (late reverb) component in the direction of desired
source is not suppressed by the spatial filter, it limits
dereverberation and interference suppression performance. Blind inverse
filtering through delayed multi-channel linear prediction (MCLP)
\[[11](#bib.bib11), [12](#bib.bib12), [13](#bib.bib13)\] in the
short-time Fourier transform (STFT) domain is an effective approach to
reduce reverberation. But MCLP has no spatial selectivity, and the
presence of noise and directional interferers causes degradation of
prediction filter estimation due to the single source assumption. Hence,
a combination of MCLP and spatial filtering with RTF (RTF-MCLP) is
considered in this paper, which would be better for dereverberation as
well as interference suppression. The RTF can also be estimated, or
specified to correspond to a particular direction, to spatially select a
desired source in the enclosure.

In MCLP, the prediction filters are estimated using a maximum likelihood
(ML) criterion with a time-varying power spectral density (PSD)
assumption for the prediction residual \[[11](#bib.bib11),
[13](#bib.bib13), [14](#bib.bib14), [15](#bib.bib15),
[16](#bib.bib16)\]. The spatial filters are often designed with a
distortion-less response constraint for the desired source direction
\[[17](#bib.bib17), [18](#bib.bib18), [10](#bib.bib10)\]. In the
stationary source case, we consider ML estimation with the
distortion-less response constraint along with time-domain short-time
auto-regressive (AR) model PSD constraint for the desired source. We
formulate an iterative solution involving MCLP reverberation
cancellation followed by minimum variance distortion-less response
(MVDR) spatial filtering, and time-domain AR model based PSD estimation
of the spatial filter output (desired signal). In the single source case
(no interference), the source RTF is estimated within the iterations of
the RTF-MCLP algorithm. Whereas in multi-source (interferer) case, we
consider the desired source RTF as known a-priori in the present
formulation. It is also possible to estimate the individual source RTFs
using constraints such as the direction of arrival, or by restricting
RTF estimation to desired source active STFT regions only.

We find that MCLP and spatial filtering can aid each other through the
iterative estimation, where MCLP can provide reduced late-reverb noise
in the estimated early component signal, the spatial filter can avoid
interfering sources from other directions. We extend the joint RTF-MCLP
formulation to dynamic sources through the linear dynamical system model
for MCLP filters, along with online MVDR spatial filtering. The MCLP
filters are estimated using ML criterion in each time frame, and the
time-dependent spatial filter for the source RTF is estimated using the
output of MCLP. In the single source case, the source RTF is also
estimated in each time frame using the MCLP residual.

### I-A Related works

A single stationary source in a noiseless reverberant environment is
considered in the early MCLP formulation of \[[12](#bib.bib12),
[11](#bib.bib11)\], using a time-varying complex Gaussian model and
maximum likelihood estimation of the source PSD. Several further works
focused on improving the prediction filter estimation using better
desired signal models \[[13](#bib.bib13), [14](#bib.bib14),
[15](#bib.bib15), [16](#bib.bib16)\], and prediction filter models
\[[19](#bib.bib19), [16](#bib.bib16)\]. An extension of the method to
noisy measurement case is considered in \[[13](#bib.bib13)\], and a
multi-source case using the blind source separation approach of
independent component analysis in \[[20](#bib.bib20),
[21](#bib.bib21)\]. Cascaded spatial filtering is used as a post filter
to reduce the residual reverberation in the MCLP enhanced signal in
\[[22](#bib.bib22), [23](#bib.bib23)\]. Though different formulations
exist to design a spatial filter \[[24](#bib.bib24), [9](#bib.bib9),
[18](#bib.bib18), [25](#bib.bib25), [10](#bib.bib10)\], among them MVDR
beamformer \[[9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10)\] is a simple and popular
approach. Spatial filtering provides spatial selectivity, and allows for
desired source estimation in recordings with multiple sources. Yet the
MCLP dereverberation gets adversely affected in a multi-source case,
which results in excess residual reverberation, and hence the post
filtering is less effective. Similar to the present work, spatial
filtering with in the MCLP iterations using a neural-network (NN) based
speech mask \[[26](#bib.bib26)\] is considered in \[[27](#bib.bib27)\],
as a pre-processing step, for an ASR task in noisy recordings. However,
no justification is available for the NN mask based approach. Instead,
we develop the scheme as a maximum likelihood solution to the joint
RTF-MCLP model of reverberant multi microphone signals.

The MCLP speech dereverberation for a dynamic source scenario has been
considered in the literature \[[28](#bib.bib28), [29](#bib.bib29),
[30](#bib.bib30), [31](#bib.bib31)\]. A recursive least squares (RLS)
formulation is proposed in \[[28](#bib.bib28)\] with source position
change detection. Further, it has been extended using a Kalman filter
approach and shown to be more effective \[[31](#bib.bib31)\]. Adaptive
estimation of time-varying channel condition is considered in
\[[29](#bib.bib29), [30](#bib.bib30)\]. However, MCLP dereverberation
for dynamic sources in the presence of interferers is not considered in
the literature. We consider RTF-MCLP along with the Kalman filter based
linear dynamical system model for both interference reduction and
desired source tracking. We show that the RTF-MCLP is readily extended
to dynamic sources, and directional interferences, as online adaptive
spatial filtering \[[32](#bib.bib32)\] of signal enhanced through the
time-varying MCLP.

## II RTF-MCLP Formulation

Consider an acoustic recording scenario using an $`M`$ element
microphone array and a single sound source inside a reverberant
enclosure with no other noise. The signal recorded at the $`m^{th}`$
microphone $`x_{m}[t]`$ can be related to the source signal $`s[t]`$
using the room impulse response (RIR) relation,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       x_{m}[t]=h_{m}[t]\circledast s[t].
       ```                                 |     | (1) |

$`h_{m}[t]`$ being the RIR between source and the $`m^{th}`$ microphone
position and $`t`$ is the discrete time index. The convolution
relationship can be expressed approximately in the STFT domain (ignoring
the cross band effects) \[[33](#bib.bib33)\] as

|     |                              |                                                                                                        |     |     |
| --- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle x_{m}[n,k]`$ | $`\displaystyle\approx\sum\limits_{p=0}^{P-1}h_{m}[p,k]s[n-p,k],`$                                     |     | (2) |
|     |                              | $`\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{p=0}^{D-1}h_{m}[p,k]s[n-p,k]+\sum\limits_{p=D}^{P-1}h_{m}[p,k]s[n-p,k],`$ |     |     |

where $`n`$ denotes the discrete time index, $`0\leq k\leq K-1`$ is the
discrete frequency bin index, and $`P`$ is the length of the RIR in STFT
domain, which is equal to the ratio of the duration of time domain
impulse response and the window shift used for STFT analysis. Blind
estimation of the STFT domain reverb filters
$`\{h_{m}[n,k],~\forall~m,k\}`$ is difficult, due to the continuous
spectro-temporal variation of the speech signal. However, we can split
the RIR into two parts: the first part in
([2](#S2.E2 "In II RTF-MCLP Formulation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
modeling the direct component and early reflections, where as the second
part models the diffuse late reverb component. We can parameterize the
late reverb component using a delayed multi channel linear prediction
(MCLP) model\[[12](#bib.bib12)\] as below:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
x_{m}[n,k]=\underbrace{\sum\limits_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}\sum\limits_{l=1}^{L}g_{m,m^{\prime}}^{*}[l,k]x_{m^{\prime}}[n-D-l,k]}_{r_{m}[n,k]}+d_{m}[n,k],
``` |  | (3) |

where the delay $`D\geq 1`$ is chosen to avoid over fitting to speech
correlations between successive STFT frames; $`D`$ controls the duration
of the early reflection component retained in prediction residual
$`d_{m}[n,k]`$.

The late reverb component does vary due to microphone position and hence
multi-microphone prediction helps in predicting out the diffuse
component. The predicted component $`r_{m}[n,k]`$ in
([3](#S2.E3 "In II RTF-MCLP Formulation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
at the $`m^{th}`$ microphone can be expressed compactly in vector form
as,

|     |                                                      |     |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       r_{m}[n,k]={\bf g}_{m}[k]^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n,k].
       ```                                                   |     | (4) |

The vector of predictor STFT samples is:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\boldsymbol{\phi}[n,k]=\left[x_{1}[n-D-1,k],\dots,x_{1}[n-D-L,k],\right.\\
\left.\dots,x_{M}[n-D-1,k],\dots,x_{M}[n-D-L,k]\right]^{T},
``` |  | (5) |

and the vector of MCLP coefficients is given by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\bf g}_{m}[k]=\left[g_{m,1}[0,k],\dots,g_{m,1}[L-1,k],\right.\\
\left.\dots,g_{m,M}[0,k],\dots,g_{m,M}[L-1,k]\right]^{T}.
``` |  | (6) |

Let $`{\bf r}[n,k]=\left[r_{1}[n,k],\dots,r_{M}[n,k]\right]^{T}`$ be the
vector form for the late reverb component at all the $`M`$ microphones,
which can be written as,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\displaystyle{\bf r}[n,k]={\bf G}[k]^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n,k],~{\bf G}[k]=\left[{\bf g}_{1}[k]~\dots{\bf g}_{M}[k]\right].
``` |  | (7) |

The MCLP parameters $`\{{\bf G}[k]\}`$ can be estimated jointly using a
stochastic formulation.

Now, to include the directionality of desired source, we approximate the
desired early component (first component in eqn.
([2](#S2.E2 "In II RTF-MCLP Formulation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")))
using a multiplicative transfer function (for a small $`D`$) as

|     |                                                |     |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       d_{m}[n,k]\approxeq H_{m}[k]s[n,k],~\forall~m.
       ```                                             |     | (8) |

In vector notation, we can write,

|     |                                       |     |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       {\bf d}[n,k]\approxeq{\bf h}[k]s[n,k]
       ```                                    |     | (9) |

where $`{\bf h}[k]=[H_{1}[k]\dots H_{M}[k]]^{T}`$ is the stack of each
mic-to-source transfer function (only early reflections), and $`s[n,k]`$
is the scalar signal STFT.

Using
([9](#S2.E9 "In II RTF-MCLP Formulation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
and
([7](#S2.E7 "In II RTF-MCLP Formulation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")),
we can write the total signal model as,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\bf x}[n,k]={\bf h}[k]s[n,k]+{\bf G}[k]^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n,k],
``` |  | (10) |

comprising early reflection part, and the predictable late reverb
component. Since we need to estimate the source signal $`s[n,k]`$, and
we don’t known $`{\bf h}[k]`$ also, we can resort to a relative transfer
function (RTF) approach using a reference microphone. i.e., the first
part of
([10](#S2.E10 "In II RTF-MCLP Formulation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
can be expressed using the RTF with respect to a reference microphone
say $`r=1`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\bf x}[n,k]={\bf a}[k]d_{1}[n,k]+{\bf G}[k]^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n,k],
``` |  | (11) |

where

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\bf a}[k]=\left[1~\frac{H_{2}[k]}{H_{1}[k]}\dots\frac{H_{M}[k]}{H_{1}[k]}\right]^{T}.
``` |  | (12) |

Let us choose a weight vector $`{{\bf w}[k]}`$ (spatial filter) such
that $`{{\bf w}}[k]^{H}{\bf a}[k]=1`$. We can re-write
([11](#S2.E11 "In II RTF-MCLP Formulation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
as,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{{\bf w}}[k]^{H}{\bf x}[n,k]=d_{1}[n,k]+{{\bf w}}[k]^{H}{\bf G}[k]^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n,k].
``` |  | (13) |

Now, we can consider the estimation of signal component $`d_{1}[n,k]`$
(desired signal) at the reference microphone. Using the multi channel
observations $`\{x_{m}[n,k],~0\leq n\leq N-1,~1\leq m\leq M\}`$, a batch
method is presented in sec.
[III](#S3 "III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"),
which is further extended to online estimation in sec.
[IV](#S4 "IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source").
For the ML solution, we consider the frequency bins to be statistically
independent and the cross-frequency effects be considered negligible.
Thus, the frequency bin index $`k`$ is omitted for brevity in the
formulation below.

## III Static Source Batch Estimation

### III-A Gaussian model of early reflection component

Consider $`d_{1}[t]`$, which is the inverse STFT of $`d_{1}[n,k]`$, to
be the speech signal with early reflections. Let $`d_{1}[t]`$ be the
output of a quasi-stationary auto regressive model of order $`Q`$, and
let $`\left\{\gamma_{nk},~\forall~k\right\}`$ denote the time-varying
power spectral density (PSD) of $`d_{1}[t]`$ at the STFT frame index
$`n`$ and frequency index $`k`$. We consider the signal
$`\{d_{1}[n,k],\forall~k\}`$ to be independent (across the time and
frequency indices $`n,k`$), circularly symmetric complex Gaussian random
variable with variance $`\gamma_{nk}`$; i.e.,
$`\mathbb{P}\left({\bf d}_{1}[k]\right)=\prod\limits_{n=1}^{N}\mathbb{P}\left(d_{1}[n,k]\right)`$,
and

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{P}\left(d_{1}[n,k]\right)=\mathcal{N}_{c}\left(d_{1}[n,k];{0},\gamma_{nk}\right).
``` |  | (14) |

The independence ignores time dependence of speech PSD, but the
frequency dependence is imposed using time domain AR model. The
discussion below is similar for each frequency bin $`k`$, and hence we
have omitted the index $`k`$ for brevity.

Using
([13](#S2.E13 "In II RTF-MCLP Formulation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
and
([14](#S3.E14 "In III-A Gaussian model of early reflection component ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")),
we can express the stochastic model of $`{\bf x}[n]`$ as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{P}\left({\bf x}[n]\left|\right.{{\bf w}},{\bf G},\boldsymbol{\phi}[n],{\gamma}_{n}\right)=\\
\frac{1}{\pi{\gamma}_{n}}\exp\left(-{\gamma}_{n}^{-1}\left|{{\bf w}}^{H}\left({\bf x}[n]-{\bf G}^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n]\right)\right|^{2}\right),
``` |  | (15) |

and

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{P}\left({\bf X}\left|\right.\boldsymbol{\Theta}\right)=\prod\limits_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathbb{P}\left({\bf x}[n]\left|\right.{{\bf w}},{\bf G},\boldsymbol{\phi}[n],{\gamma}_{n}\right),
``` |  | (16) |

where
$`\boldsymbol{\Theta}=\{{\bf w},{\bf G},\boldsymbol{\gamma}=\{{\gamma}_{n},~\forall~n\}\}`$
is the set of all parameters to be estimated given the multi-microphone
signals $`{\bf X}=\left[{\bf x}[0],\dots,{\bf x}[N-1]\right]`$.

### III-B Parameter Estimation

Using the above stochastic formulation of $`{\bf x}[n]`$, we consider
maximum likelihood (ML) parameter estimation:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}=\underset{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}{\arg\max}~~\mathbb{P}\left({\bf X}\left|\right.\boldsymbol{\Theta}\right).
``` |  | (17) |

Equivalently, negative logarithm of the likelihood function can be
minimized. i.e.,
$`\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\Theta})\propto-\log p({\bf X}|\boldsymbol{\Theta})`$,
where

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\displaystyle\hskip-4.0pt\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\Theta})\triangleq\sum\limits_{n=0}^{N-1}\left[\log\gamma_{n}+\gamma_{n}^{-1}\left|{{\bf w}}^{H}\left({\bf x}[n]-{\bf G}^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n]\right)\right|^{2}\right].
``` |  | (18) |

Direct minimization of $`\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\Theta})`$ with respect
to the variables $`\{\gamma_{n},~\forall~n\}`$, $`{\bf w}`$ and
$`{\bf G}`$ is not possible, because of the inter-dependencies between
them. Instead, we consider a coordinate descent approach, in which the
variables are successively optimized in a sequential, iterative manner.

#### III-B1 Estimation of MCLP filters ($`{\bf G}`$)

The part of cost function $`\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\Theta})`$ relevant
for the estimation of $`{\bf G}`$ is,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}({\bf G})=\sum\limits_{n=0}^{N-1}\hat{\gamma}_{n}^{-1}\left|\hat{{\bf w}}^{H}\left({\bf x}[n]-{\bf G}^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n]\right)\right|^{2}.
``` |  | (19) |

Since we are estimating the parameters sequentially, let
$`\hat{\gamma}_{n}`$ and $`\hat{{\bf w}}`$ be the estimates from
previous iteration. Using the following definitions

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle{\bf R}_{\phi\phi}\triangleq\sum\limits_{n=0}^{N-1}\hat{\gamma}_{n}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n]\boldsymbol{\phi}[n]^{H},~{\bf R}_{\phi x}\triangleq\sum\limits_{n=0}^{N-1}\hat{\gamma}_{n}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n]{\bf x}[n]^{H},`$ |  | (20) |

and $`{\bf W}\triangleq{{\bf w}}{{\bf w}}^{H}`$, the term dependent on
MCLP filter $`{\bf G}`$ in the likelihood function of eqn.
([19](#S3.E19 "In III-B1 Estimation of MCLP filters (𝐆) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
can be written, using the trace notation, as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L({\bf G})}=tr\left(\left[{\bf G}^{H}{\bf R}_{\phi\phi}{\bf G}-{\bf R}_{\phi x}^{H}{\bf G}-{\bf G}^{H}{\bf R}_{\phi x}\right]{\bf W}\right).
``` |  | (21) |

Taking the derivative of eqn.
([21](#S3.E21 "In III-B1 Estimation of MCLP filters (𝐆) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
with respect to the matrix variable $`{\bf G}`$ and equating to zero, we
get

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\bf W}\left[{\bf G}^{H}{\bf R}_{\phi\phi}-{\bf R}_{\phi x}^{H}\right]={\bf 0}.
``` |  | (22) |

The solution for this is not unique, since
$`{\bf W}={\bf w}{\bf w}^{H}`$ is a rank-one matrix, and any matrix in
the null space of $`{\bf W}`$ will satisfy the above equality. However,
since it is iterative optimization, we can consider an approximate
solution of

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\left[{\bf G}^{H}{\bf R}_{\phi\phi}-{\bf R}_{\phi x}^{H}\right]={\bf 0},
``` |  | (23) |

to lead to a useful solution through the iterations. The MCLP filter
matrix $`{\bf G}`$ solution is obtained as,

|     |                                                        |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \hat{{\bf G}}={\bf R}_{\phi\phi}^{-1}{\bf R}_{\phi x}.
       ```                                                     |     | (24) |

i.e., the estimate for $`\hat{{\bf G}}`$ is obtained similar to the WPE
method \[[11](#bib.bib11)\], but as we show later in sec.
[III-B4](#S3.SS2.SSS4 "III-B4 Estimation of Desired Signal Variance (𝛾_𝑛) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"),
solution for the weight parameter $`{\gamma}_{n}`$ is different in the
present approach.

#### III-B2 Steering Vector $`({\bf a})`$

Consider the prediction residual computed using the estimate for
$`{\bf G}`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{{\bf d}}[n]={\bf x}[n]-\hat{{\bf G}}^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n].
``` |  | (25) |

We note that, the estimate $`\hat{{\bf d}}[n]`$ comprises of the desired
early component signal $`{\bf d}[n]={\bf a}d_{1}[n]`$ and also the
residual reverberation $`\tilde{{\bf r}}[n]`$. Assuming the two
components to be uncorrelated, we can write,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle{\bf R}_{{\bf d}{\bf d}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left\{\hat{{\bf d}}[n]\hat{{\bf d}}[n]^{H}\right\}`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\approx{\bf a}{\bf a}^{H}\mathbb{E}\left\{|d_{1}[n]|^{2}\right\}+\mathbb{E}\left\{\tilde{{\bf r}}[n]\tilde{{\bf r}}[n]^{H}\right\}.`$ |  | (26) |

Because the energy of residual reverberation $`\tilde{{\bf r}}[n]`$ is
smaller than that of desired signal, we can ignore it and we can
estimate the RTF $`{\bf a}`$ from first column of the correlation matrix
\[[8](#bib.bib8)\]:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{{\bf a}}=\frac{{\bf R}_{{\bf d}{\bf d}}{\bf e}_{1}}{{\bf e}_{1}^{H}{\bf R}_{{\bf d}{\bf d}}{\bf e}_{1}},
``` |  | (27) |

where $`{\bf e}_{1}`$ is the first column of the $`M\times M`$ identity
matrix. A different estimate based on the eigen vector corresponding to
largest eigen value of $`{\bf R}_{{\bf d}{\bf d}}`$ can also be used
\[[34](#bib.bib34)\]. (Different methods of computing RTF are not
considered at present).

#### III-B3 Estimation of Spatial Filter $`({\bf w})`$

The term dependent on spatial filter $`{\bf w}`$ in the likelihood
function
([18](#S3.E18 "In III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
is,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}({\bf w})={\bf w}^{H}\left[\sum\limits_{n=1}^{N}\hat{\gamma}_{n}^{-1}\hat{{\bf d}}[n]\hat{{\bf d}}[n]^{H}\right]{\bf w}\triangleq{\bf w}^{H}{\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf d}}\hat{{\bf d}}}{\bf w}.
``` |  | (28) |

Using the distortion-less response constraint of
([13](#S2.E13 "In II RTF-MCLP Formulation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")),
the ML estimation problem can be stated as,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\displaystyle\mbox{minimize}~\left\{{\bf w}^{H}{\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf d}}\hat{{\bf d}}}{\bf w}\right\},\mbox{ s.t. }{\bf w}^{H}\hat{{\bf a}}=1.
``` |  | (29) |

This is similar to the MVDR formulation, where
$`{\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf d}}\hat{{\bf d}}}`$ denotes the spatial covariance
matrix of the filter input. Solution to
([29](#S3.E29 "In III-B3 Estimation of Spatial Filter (𝐰) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
can be obtained as \[[10](#bib.bib10)\],

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{{\bf w}}=\frac{{\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf d}}\hat{{\bf d}}}^{-1}\hat{{\bf a}}}{\hat{{\bf a}}^{H}{\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf d}}\hat{{\bf d}}}^{-1}\hat{{\bf a}}}.
``` |  | (30) |

As noted earlier, the estimated early reflection signal component
$`\hat{{\bf d}}[n]`$ also includes some amount of residual reverberation
$`\tilde{{\bf r}}[n]`$ (since it is diffuse). Using the model in
([11](#S2.E11 "In II RTF-MCLP Formulation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")),
the optimization criterion
([29](#S3.E29 "In III-B3 Estimation of Spatial Filter (𝐰) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
can be re-stated as,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\displaystyle\mbox{minimize}~\left\{{\bf w}^{H}{\bf R}_{\tilde{{\bf r}}\tilde{{\bf r}}}{\bf w}\right\},\mbox{ s.t. }{\bf w}^{H}\hat{{\bf a}}=1.
``` |  | (31) |

We assume the spatial correlation matrix of the residual reverberation
component $`{\bf R}_{\tilde{{\bf r}}\tilde{{\bf r}}}`$ to be
proportional to the spatial correlation matrix of the predicted
reverberation component
$`\hat{{\bf r}}[n]=\hat{{\bf G}}^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n]`$, i.e.,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\bf R}_{\tilde{{\bf r}}\tilde{{\bf r}}}\propto{\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf r}}\hat{{\bf r}}}=\sum\limits_{n=1}^{N}\hat{\gamma}_{n}^{-1}\hat{{\bf r}}[n]\hat{{\bf r}}[n]^{H}.
``` |  | (32) |

The above assumption is justified since the reverberation component and
the residual reverberation component are both assumed to be diffuse and
spatially homogeneous \[[22](#bib.bib22)\], in general sound fields.
Thus, the corresponding spatial filter solution is,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{{\bf w}}=\frac{{\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf r}}\hat{{\bf r}}}^{-1}\hat{{\bf a}}}{\hat{{\bf a}}^{H}{\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf r}}\hat{{\bf r}}}^{-1}\hat{{\bf a}}}.
``` |  | (33) |

We use the spatial filter in
([33](#S3.E33 "In III-B3 Estimation of Spatial Filter (𝐰) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
for experimentation in this paper, since the solution in
([30](#S3.E30 "In III-B3 Estimation of Spatial Filter (𝐰) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
is found to be sensitive to errors in RTF estimation $`\hat{{\bf a}}`$.

#### III-B4 Estimation of Desired Signal Variance $`(\gamma_{n})`$

The part of objective function of
([18](#S3.E18 "In III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
dependent on the STFT signal variance $`\gamma_{n}`$ is,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}(\gamma_{n})=\log\gamma_{n}+\gamma_{n}^{-1}|\hat{d}_{1}[n]|^{2},~\forall n,
``` |  | (34) |

where
$`\hat{d}_{1}[n]=\hat{{\bf w}}^{H}\left({\bf x}[n]-\hat{{\bf G}}^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n]\right)`$
is the spatial filtered MCLP residual. Minimizer of the objective
function is the energy of signal $`\hat{d}_{1}[n]`$, i.e.,
$`|\hat{d}_{1}[n]|^{2}`$. This is an instantaneous estimate for each
STFT bin $`k`$. We can make the variance estimate more consistent by
exploiting the correlation across frequency bins, i.e., estimating a
smoothed PSD of $`d_{1}[n]`$. We resort to time-domain low-order AR
modeling of the residual signal $`\hat{d}_{1}[n,k]`$, which is obtained
after computing the spatial filtered residue signal for each frequency
bin $`k`$. We choose a fixed predictor order of $`Q=21`$ for the AR
model, and the estimated PSD at time index $`n`$ is given by
\[[35](#bib.bib35)\]

|     |                                                             |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       H_{n}[z]=\frac{G_{n}}{1-\sum\limits_{q=1}^{Q}a_{pn}z^{-p}}.
       ```                                                          |     | (35) |

The frequency response of the time domain AR model $`H_{n}[z]`$ is used
to derive the estimate for $`\gamma_{n}`$ as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{\gamma}_{nk}={\left|H_{n}[z_{k}]\right|^{2}},~z_{k}=e^{-j2\pi k/K}.
``` |  | (36) |

We found that this estimate is better than the direct ML estimate
$`\left|\hat{d}_{1}[n,k]\right|^{2}`$ for $`\gamma_{nk}`$.

### III-C Iterative Parameter Estimation of RTF-MCLP

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 1: Block diagram of the RTF-MCLP algorithm

A block diagram of the joint estimation of MCLP and RTF, iteratively, is
shown in Fig.
[1](#S3.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ III-C Iterative Parameter Estimation of RTF-MCLP ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source").
At iteration $`i`$, we utilize the past estimate of desired speech PSD
$`\hat{\gamma}_{nk}`$ and compute the MCLP filter using
([24](#S3.E24 "In III-B1 Estimation of MCLP filters (𝐆) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")).
Then the prediction residual $`\hat{d}_{m}[n,k]`$ for each microphone
$`m`$ is computed for each frequency bin $`k`$. This prediction residual
is then used to estimate the RTF $`{\bf a}[k]`$, and the spatial filter
$`{\bf w}[k]`$ and desired signal $`\hat{d}_{1}[n,k]`$ are obtained. The
output of spatial filter $`\hat{d}_{1}[n,k]`$ is then used to compute
the desired signal PSD for the next iteration. The reverberant signal
$`{\bf x}[n,k]`$ itself is considered as initialization of
$`\hat{{\bf d}}[n,k]`$ for the first iteration, and the initial
estimates for steering vector and the spatial filter are computed.
Output of the spatial filter is then used to compute initial estimate of
desired signal PSD $`\gamma_{nk}`$.

### III-D Desired Source Selection of Multiple Sources

In
([11](#S2.E11 "In II RTF-MCLP Formulation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")),
we have considered a single source and a spatial filter to enhance the
MCLP performance. Let us now consider multiple sources $`s=1,2,\dots,S`$
contributing to the $`M`$ microphone signals. However, the diffuse late
reverb component due to all the $`S`$ sources is predictable by MCLP
\[[20](#bib.bib20)\], the prediction residual contains early reflection
components due to all the sources. Thus,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\bf x}[n,k]=\sum_{s=1}^{S}{\bf a}_{s}[k]d_{s1}[n,k]+{\bf r}[n,k],
``` |  | (37) |

where $`{\bf a}_{s}[k]`$ is the RTF vector for the source $`s`$. When we
want to estimate a desired source ($`s^{*}`$) among the multiple
sources, we assume the corresponding RTF to be known a-priori, i.e.,
$`{\bf a}_{s^{*}}[k]`$ is known¹¹ 1 It is possible to select a desired
source using other criteria such as dominant energy, etc.. Using the
algorithm described in sec.
[III-C](#S3.SS3 "III-C Iterative Parameter Estimation of RTF-MCLP ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"),
the desired signal is estimated subject to the constraint
$`{\bf w}[k]^{H}{\bf a}_{s^{*}}[k]=1`$. Since the PSD $`\gamma_{nk}`$ is
estimated after spatial filtering, it corresponds to the desired source
through successive iterations. MCLP estimation with the constraint of
desired source signal PSD as the estimate for $`\gamma_{nk}`$ improves
estimation of the early component iteratively. The noise spatial
covariance matrix computed for spatial filtering in
([31](#S3.E31 "In III-B3 Estimation of Spatial Filter (𝐰) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
includes the late reverb components of desired source and the
interferers. Hence, minimization of noise power in spatial filtering
suppresses the interfering sources along with the residual reverberation
of the desired source.

## IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation

The batch method described earlier can be considered as comprising of
two stages: the MCLP dereverberation and distortion-less response
spatial filtering. The two stages aid each other through the iterations,
one reducing the effect of diffuse reverb component and the other
reducing the effect of interfering source/noise. The advantage of this
joint optimization can be exploited for spatial filtering of a moving
source also. But, the moving source based MCLP filtering requires a
time-varying MCLP model, so that the predictors are optimally adapted.
The issue to be resolved for a moving source is that of changing the RTF
with respect to microphones and further its effect on the MCLP itself.

Since our static analysis is based on STFT, even for the moving source
case, the same linear signal model is used with a slight generalization:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
x_{m}[n,k]=d_{m}[n,k]+{\bf g}_{m,n}[k]^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n,k],
``` |  | (38) |

where the MCLP coefficients $`{\bf g}_{m,n}[k]`$ are dependent on the
STFT frame index $`n`$. In vector form, we can express the RTF-MCLP
model as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\bf x}[n,k]={\bf a}_{n}[k]d_{1}[n,k]+{\bf G}_{n}[k]^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n,k].
``` |  | (39) |

We note that the direct ML estimation using the distortion-less response
constraint for the spatial filter, and a linear dynamical system model
for MCLP will be intractable. Hence, we consider the desired signal
component $`{\bf d}[n,k]={\bf a}_{n}[k]d_{1}[n,k]`$ to be an isotropic
complex Gaussian random variable,
$`\mathbb{P}\left({\bf d}[n,k]\right)=\mathcal{N}_{c}\left({\bf 0},\gamma_{nk}{\bf I}\right)`$,
and hence

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{P}\left({\bf x}[n,k]\right)=\mathcal{N}_{c}\left({\bf G}_{n}[k]^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n,k],\gamma_{nk}{\bf I}\right).
``` |  | (40) |

Now we formulate an optimum time-varying MCLP using a linear dynamic
system approach and also perform online spatial filtering; we can then
estimate the variable $`\gamma_{nk}`$ using the spatial filter output
similar to the batch method.

### IV-A Time-varying MCLP

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 2: Graphical model of the $`M`$ microphone observations.

We consider a Gaussian innovation model for the time-varying MCLP
coefficients $`\{{\bf g}_{m,n}[k],~\forall~m\}`$ given by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\bf g}_{m,n}[k]={\bf g}_{m,n-1}[k]+{\bf i}_{m,n}[k],~\forall~m\in\left[1~M\right],
``` |  | (41) |

where the innovation term $`{\bf i}_{m,n}[k]`$ is a complex Gaussian
distributed random variable with mean zero and covariance matrix
$`\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{nk}`$. The innovation is i.i.d (independent and
identically distributed) across all the microphones, i.e.,
$`{\bf i}_{m,n}[k]=\mathcal{N}_{c}({\bf i}_{m,n}[k];{\bf 0},\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{nk}),~\forall~m`$.
We consider a diagonal covariance matrix for the innovation term, for
the sake of simplicity
$`\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{nk}\triangleq diag(\lambda_{n,k,i})`$. Thus, the
prediction coefficients can vary independently for each frequency bin,
each microphone $`m`$ and time frame $`n`$. As earlier, the frequency
bin index $`k`$ is omitted below for brevity.

We consider maximum likelihood criterion for estimating the time-varying
parameters. At time frame $`n`$, we consider the optimization problem,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mbox{maximize}~\left\{\log\mathbb{P}\left({\bf X}_{0:n}\left|\right.\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{n}\right)\right\},
``` |  | (42) |

where $`{\bf X}_{0:n}=\left[{\bf x}[0],\dots,{\bf x}[n]\right]`$,
$`\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{n}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{0:n}`$, where
$`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{n}=\{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{n},{\gamma}_{n}\}`$.
We consider a time recursive solution,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mbox{maximize}~\left\{\log\mathbb{P}\left({\bf x}[n]\left|\right.{\bf X}_{0:n-1},\hat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}_{n-1},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{n}\right)\right\}.
``` |  | (43) |

The problem can be solved sequentially using the EM algorithm
\[[36](#bib.bib36)\]. The E-step requires computation of the posterior
distribution
$`\mathbb{P}\left({\bf G}_{n}\left|\right.{\bf X}_{0:n},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{n}\right)`$.
Using the i.i.d assumption in
([40](#S4.E40 "In IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")),
([41](#S4.E41 "In IV-A Time-varying MCLP ‣ IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
over the microphone index $`m`$, we can show that

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{P}\left({\bf G}_{n}\left|\right.{\bf X}_{0:n},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{n}\right)=\prod_{m=1}^{M}\mathbb{P}\left({\bf g}_{m,n}\left|\right.{\bf X}_{0:n},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{n}\right),\mbox{where}
``` |  |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{P}\left({\bf g}_{m,n}\left|\right.{\bf X}_{0:n},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{n}\right)\propto\mathbb{P}\left(x_{m}[n],{\bf g}_{m,n}\left|\right.{\bf X}_{0:n-1},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{n}\right),
``` |  | (44) |

and

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{P}\left(x_{m}[n],{\bf g}_{m,n}\left|\right.{\bf X}_{0:n-1},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{n}\right)=\\
\mathbb{P}\left(x_{m}[n]\left|\right.{\bf g}_{m,n},\gamma_{n}\right)\mathbb{P}\left({\bf g}_{m,n}\left|\right.{\bf X}_{0:n-1},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{n}\right).
``` |  | (45) |

The distribution
$`\mathbb{P}\left({\bf g}_{m,n}\left|\right.{\bf X}_{0:n-1},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{n}\right)`$
is obtained after marginalizing over the random variable
$`{\bf g}_{m,n-1}`$, and it corresponds to a Gaussian distribution. Let

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{P}\left({\bf g}_{m,n}\left|\right.{\bf X}_{0:n-1},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{n}\right)=\mathcal{N}_{c}\left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m,n|n-1},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{n|n-1}\right),
``` |  | (46) |

using
([41](#S4.E41 "In IV-A Time-varying MCLP ‣ IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")),
we can show that

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m,n\left|\right.n-1}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m,n-1\left|\right.n-1},~\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{n\left|\right.n-1}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{n-1\left|\right.n-1}+\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{n},`$ |  | (47) |

i.e., mean is unchanged but the covariance is getting corrected.
Similarly, we have the posterior distribution

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left({\bf g}_{m,n}\left|\right.{\bf X}_{0:n},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{n}\right)=\mathcal{N}_{c}\left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m,n|n},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{n|n}\right),
``` |  | (48) |
|  |
``` math
\displaystyle\mbox{where}~\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{n\left|\right.n}=\left[\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{n\left|\right.n-1}^{-1}+\gamma_{n}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n]\boldsymbol{\phi}[n]^{H}\right]^{-1},~\mbox{and}
``` |  |  |
|  |
``` math
\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m,n\left|\right.n}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{n\left|\right.n}\left[\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{n\left|\right.n-1}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m,n\left|\right.n-1}+\gamma_{n}^{-1}x_{m}^{*}[n]\boldsymbol{\phi}[n]\right],
``` |  |  |

where $`x_{m}^{*}[n]`$ is the complex conjugate of the scalar
$`x_{m}[n]`$. The equations in
([48](#S4.E48 "In IV-A Time-varying MCLP ‣ IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
can be simplified and rewritten \[[37](#bib.bib37)\] as,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle{e}_{m}[n]\triangleq x_{m}[n]-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m,n|n-1}^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n],~\forall~m`$ |  | (49) |
|  | $`\displaystyle{\bf K}[n]=\frac{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{n|n-1}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n]}{\gamma_{n}+\boldsymbol{\phi}[n]^{H}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{n|n-1}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n]},`$ |  | (50) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{n|n}=\left[{\bf I}-{\bf K}[n]\boldsymbol{\phi}[n]^{H}\right]\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{n|n-1},`$ |  | (51) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m,n|n}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m,n|n-1}+{\bf K}[n]{e}_{m}^{*}[n],~\forall~m.`$ |  | (52) |

The computational expressions are similar to the traditional Kalman
filter estimation, for each $`m`$. The posterior mean is taken as the
estimated prediction filter at time frame $`n`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{{\bf g}}_{m,n}\triangleq\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m,n|n},~\forall~m,
``` |  | (53) |

and the estimates of early and the late reverb components are computed
as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{{r}}_{m}[n]=\hat{{\bf g}}_{m,n}^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n],~\mbox{and }\hat{{d}}_{m}[n]={x}_{m}[n]-\hat{{r}}_{m}[n].`$ |  | (54) |

The computations in
([47](#S4.E47 "In IV-A Time-varying MCLP ‣ IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")),
([49](#S4.E49 "In IV-A Time-varying MCLP ‣ IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
require estimates of the parameters
$`\gamma_{n},\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{n}`$. We use the estimate
$`\hat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}_{n-1}`$ of the previous time step in the
computations of
([47](#S4.E47 "In IV-A Time-varying MCLP ‣ IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")),
and the parameter $`\gamma_{n}`$ is computed after online spatial
filtering similar to eqn.
([36](#S3.E36 "In III-B4 Estimation of Desired Signal Variance (𝛾_𝑛) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")).

### IV-B Online spatial filtering

The optimization problem in eqn.
([31](#S3.E31 "In III-B3 Estimation of Spatial Filter (𝐰) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
can be modified for the online estimation case as,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{{\bf w}}_{n}=\underset{{\bf w}_{n}}{\arg\min}~{\bf w}_{n}^{H}{\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf r}}\hat{{\bf r}}}[n]{\bf w}_{n},`$ |  | (55) |

subject to the constraint $`{\bf w}_{n}^{H}{\bf a}_{n}=1`$. A running
estimate of the covariance matrix
$`{\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf r}}\hat{{\bf r}}}[n]`$ is computed using recursive
averaging with smoothing constant $`\alpha_{1}`$ as,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf r}}\hat{{\bf r}}}[n]=(1-\alpha_{1}){\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf r}}\hat{{\bf r}}}[n-1]+\alpha_{1}\gamma_{n}^{-1}\hat{{\bf r}}[n]\hat{{\bf r}}[n]^{H}.
``` |  | (56) |

The solution to
([55](#S4.E55 "In IV-B Online spatial filtering ‣ IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
is computed similar to
([33](#S3.E33 "In III-B3 Estimation of Spatial Filter (𝐰) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")),

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{{\bf w}}_{n}=\frac{{\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf r}}\hat{{\bf r}}}[n]^{-1}{\bf a}_{n}}{{\bf a}_{n}^{H}{\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf r}}\hat{{\bf r}}}[n]^{-1}{\bf a}_{n}}.
``` |  | (57) |

### IV-C Parameter Estimation

#### IV-C1 Gaussian Innovation Covariance

The matrix $`\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{n}=diag({{\lambda}}_{n,i})`$ is the
covariance of innovations in MCLP coefficients, which can be estimated
as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{{\lambda}}_{n,i}=\frac{1}{M}\sum\limits_{m=1}^{M}\mathbb{E}\left\{\left|{\bf g}_{m,n}[i]-{\bf g}_{m,n-1}[i]\right|^{2}\right\},
``` |  | (58) |

where $`{\bf g}_{m,n}[i]`$ is the $`i^{th}`$ entry of the vector
$`{\bf g}_{m,n}`$, and the expectation is taken with respect to the
joint distribution
$`\mathbb{P}\left({\bf G}_{n},{\bf G}_{n-1}\left|\right.{\bf X}_{0:n},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{n}\right)`$.
To avoid the computation of joint distribution, which requires backward
recursion \[[37](#bib.bib37)\], we consider a simpler estimate based on
the changing mean vector:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{{\lambda}}_{n,i}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m,n|n}[i]-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m,n-1|n-1}[i]\right|^{2}+\epsilon,
``` |  | (59) |

where $`\epsilon`$ is a small positive constant.

#### IV-C2 Desired Signal Variance

$`\gamma_{nk}`$ is related to the PSD of the desired signal
$`d_{1}[n,k]`$. However, estimation of $`\hat{{d}}_{1}[n,k]`$ requires
an estimate of $`{\bf\gamma}_{nk}`$. To avoid this dependence, the
a-priori desired signal estimate

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tilde{d}_{1}[n,k]=\hat{{\bf w}}_{n-1}[k]^{H}\left({\bf x}[n,k]-\hat{{\bf G}}_{n-1}[k]^{H}\boldsymbol{\phi}[n,k]\right),
``` |  | (60) |

is used to compute the time domain AR model
([35](#S3.E35 "In III-B4 Estimation of Desired Signal Variance (𝛾_𝑛) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
and the desired signal PSD estimate is obtained using
([36](#S3.E36 "In III-B4 Estimation of Desired Signal Variance (𝛾_𝑛) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")).

#### IV-C3 Relative transfer function $`({\bf a}_{n})`$

The time dependent RTF is computed using the estimated early reflection
component $`\hat{{\bf d}}[n]`$. The spatial cross correlation matrix,
similar to
([26](#S3.Ex2 "In III-B2 Steering Vector (𝐚) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")),
is computed using recursive averaging with a smoothing parameter
$`\alpha_{2}`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle{\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf d}}\hat{{\bf d}}}[n]=(1-\alpha_{2}){\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf d}}\hat{{\bf d}}}[n-1]+\alpha_{2}\hat{{\bf d}}[n]\hat{{\bf d}}[n]^{H}.`$ |  | (61) |

The estimate for RTF is computed similar to
([27](#S3.E27 "In III-B2 Steering Vector (𝐚) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{{\bf a}}_{n}=\frac{{\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf d}}\hat{{\bf d}}}[n]{\bf e}_{1}}{{\bf e}_{1}^{H}{\bf R}_{\hat{{\bf d}}\hat{{\bf d}}}[n]{\bf e}_{1}}.
``` |  | (62) |

Care must be taken in updating the RTF, since STFT bins with silence or
dominant diffuse component in the estimated early reflection component
can drift the RTF from the actual signal source. We determine the RTF
update based on ratio of the average energies of $`\hat{{\bf d}}[n]`$
and $`\hat{{\bf r}}[n]`$, when it is greater than $`0.1`$.

### IV-D Online RTF-MCLP Algorithm

The algorithm for online RTF-MCLP is shown in Alg.
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ IV-D Online RTF-MCLP Algorithm ‣ IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source").
The spatial filter, and the MCLP prediction filter computed at the time
index $`n-1`$ are used to obtain the a-priori desired signal estimate,
which is then used to compute the desired signal variance. Given the
desired signal variance, the posterior distribution parameters of the
MCLP filters are computed and estimates of the multi channel early
component and late reverberation component are computed. The estimated
early reflection component is then used to update the RTF, and the late
reverb component is used to update the noise covariance matrix. The
spatial filter is then recomputed and the filter output is taken as the
desired signal.

1: Initialize $`\hat{{\bf w}}_{-1}[k]={\bf 1}/\sqrt{M},~\forall~k`$,
$`\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m,-1|-1}[k]={\bf 0},~\forall m,k\}`$,
$`\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{-1|-1}[k]=\eta{\bf I}`$, $`\eta=10^{-3}`$.

2: for $`n=0:N-1`$ do

3:   Compute the a-priori signal estimate using
([60](#S4.E60 "In IV-C2 Desired Signal Variance ‣ IV-C Parameter Estimation ‣ IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"))
$`\forall k`$.

4:   Compute the desired signal variance $`\hat{\gamma}_{nk}`$ using
([36](#S3.E36 "In III-B4 Estimation of Desired Signal Variance (𝛾_𝑛) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")).

5:   for $`k=0:K/2`$ do

6:    Compute
$`\mathbb{P}\left({\bf g}_{m,n}[k]\left|\right.{\bf X}_{0:n-1}[k]\right),\forall~m`$
using
([47](#S4.E47 "In IV-A Time-varying MCLP ‣ IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")).

7:    Compute
$`\mathbb{P}\left({\bf g}_{m,n}[k]\left|\right.{\bf X}_{0:n}[k]\right),\forall~m`$
using
([49](#S4.E49 "In IV-A Time-varying MCLP ‣ IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")).

8:    Update the prediction filter using
([53](#S4.E53 "In IV-A Time-varying MCLP ‣ IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")).

9:    Compute $`\hat{{\bf d}}[n,k]`$, and $`\hat{{\bf r}}[n,k]`$ using
([54](#S4.E54 "In IV-A Time-varying MCLP ‣ IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")).

10:    Update the RTF $`\hat{{\bf a}}_{n}[k]`$ using
([62](#S4.E62 "In IV-C3 Relative transfer function (𝐚_𝑛) ‣ IV-C Parameter Estimation ‣ IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")).

11:    Update the noise covariance matrix using
([56](#S4.E56 "In IV-B Online spatial filtering ‣ IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")).

12:    Compute the spatial filter $`\hat{{\bf w}}_{n}[k]`$ using
([57](#S4.E57 "In IV-B Online spatial filtering ‣ IV Dynamic Source Online Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")).

13:    Compute the spatial filtered signal

|     |                                                               |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \hat{{d}}_{1}[n,k]=\hat{{\bf w}}_{n}[k]^{H}\hat{{\bf d}}[n,k]
       ```                                                            |     | (63) |

14:   end for

15: end for

Algorithm 1 Online joint spatial filtering and MCLP

## V Experiments and Results

First we study the performance of the joint RTF-MCLP model for signal
estimation in a batch mode (static sources but non-stationary speech),
and later present the results for a dynamic source. We consider the
recording setup shown in Fig.
[3](#S5.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source");
we generate simulated room impulse responses, using the image method
\[[38](#bib.bib38), [39](#bib.bib39)\], for each of the mics. A uniform
circular array (UCA) with $`4`$ microphones and of radius $`0.1~m`$ is
considered for the recording. Center of the array is placed at
coordinates $`[2.3,2.45,1.1]~m`$ with respect to the lower left corner
of the enclosure. Desired source is assumed to be at the position
$`[2.3,3.45,1.1]~m`$, and an interferer at $`[3.007,3.157,1.1]~m`$ (both
at a distance of $`1~m`$ from the center of array), and the
reverberation time of the enclosure is $`RT60=0.6~s`$, unless otherwise
stated.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

(a)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

(b)

Fig. 3: Room setup for simulated impulse responses. (a) Stationary
source case, (b) Dynamic source case. Black: UCA mics located at
$`[2.3,2.45,1.1]~m`$ for both cases.

Clean signals from the TIMIT database \[[40](#bib.bib40)\] are convolved
with the simulated RIRs to generate the reverberant microphone signals.
Ten signals ($`5`$ each from male and female speakers) are used for the
evaluation. Interference signal is also speech signal from different
from the target signal. STFT analysis of mic signal is carried out using
a Hann window of size $`32~ms`$, and a successive frame overlap of
$`75\%`$. We consider the size of discrete Fourier transform in STFT to
be the same as window size (equal to $`512`$ for the signal sampling
rate of $`16~KHz`$).

We study the performance of the proposed dereverberation approach using
the objective measure of frequency weighted signal-to-noise ratio
(FwSNR) \[[41](#bib.bib41)\], and subjective performance measures of
“perceptual evaluation of speech quality” (PESQ) \[[42](#bib.bib42)\]
and the “short-time objective intelligibility” (STOI)
\[[43](#bib.bib43)\]. PESQ is bounded between $`[1-5]`$ with $`5`$ being
closest to clean speech. STOI lies between $`[0-1]`$ with $`1`$
indicating best intelligibility. FwSNR is computed using the evaluation
toolbox provided in \[[44](#bib.bib44)\], and STOI is computed using the
auditory modeling toolbox \[[45](#bib.bib45)\]. Processed speech
examples are available online at www.ece.iisc.ernet.in/~sraj/dMCLP.html.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 4: Cascaded MCLP and RTF based spatial filtering scheme
\[[22](#bib.bib22), [23](#bib.bib23)\] for performance comparison with
RTF-MCLP.

We compare the performance of the new RTF-MCLP with (i) MCLP method with
AR source prior \[[13](#bib.bib13)\] (first block in
Fig.[4](#S5.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")),
(ii) a separate cascade of the MVDR beamformer for the MCLP output
\[[23](#bib.bib23), [22](#bib.bib22)\] (C-RTF-MCLP) as shown in
Fig.[4](#S5.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"),
and (iii) the super directive beamformer (SDB) \[[9](#bib.bib9),
[46](#bib.bib46)\]. For the MCLP method, the autocorrelation function
required for source AR estimation is computed by averaging the
autocorrelation function of the multi-channel prediction residual
signals. For the MVDR beamformer post filter, the noise covariance
matrix is computed using the reverberation component estimated using the
MCLP, and the RTF is estimated using
([27](#S3.E27 "In III-B2 Steering Vector (𝐚) ‣ III-B Parameter Estimation ‣ III Static Source Batch Estimation ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")).
SDB is implemented assuming free field RTF $`{\bf a}`$ (vector
$`{\bf a}`$ corresponds to the direct path only) and the microphone
placement (diffuse noise spatial covariance matrix) is assumed known
a-priori.

Fig.
[5](#S5.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ V-A Stationary source, batch processing ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")(a)
shows the output of the MCLP filters in RTF-MCLP scheme with RIR as the
input, in time domain. The filters are estimated first using a speech
signal, and then used to obtain the output RIR considering it as the
microphone signal. We see from estimated RIR that the direct component
and the first few early reflection peaks are retained; they also match
the input RIR in amplitude and time-location. The reflection components
beyond $`\approx 16~ms`$ are suppressed significantly after the MCLP
filtering, i.e., the effective duration of RIR after the MCLP filter
stage is $`\approx 16~ms`$. Since the window size chosen for the STFT
analysis is $`32~ms`$, we can see that the RTF approximation in the STFT
domain is valid, only with some residual reverberation noise. Fig.
[5](#S5.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ V-A Stationary source, batch processing ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")(b)
shows the corresponding energy decay curve (EDC), we can see that the
room reflection components over long-term of $`16-220~ms`$ are
suppressed. However, there is an increase in the reflection component
energy beyond $`\approx 220~ms`$, but it is below $`-20~dB`$ level. Fig.
[5](#S5.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ V-A Stationary source, batch processing ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")(b)
also shows EDC for the effective RIR after the spatial filter. We see
that the level of residual reverberation decreases after the spatial
filter, and we found that there is a small improvement near the early
reflection components also.

[6](#S5.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ V-A1 RTF-MCLP Algorithm Parameters ‣ V-A Stationary source, batch processing ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")
shows the performance measures for different algorithm parameters. We
see that (i) spatial filter in combination with the MCLP filter improves
the MCLP performance, and (ii) the joint estimation in RTF-MCLP performs
better than the cascade approach of C-RTF-MCLP, particularly for the
perceptual measures of PESQ and STOI, though minimal for FwSNR. Fig.
[6](#S5.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ V-A1 RTF-MCLP Algorithm Parameters ‣ V-A Stationary source, batch processing ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")(a-c)
show the performance measures for increasing value of prediction order
$`L`$. We see that peak performance is obtained for
$`L=12\mbox{ to }16`$, indicating the structure of diffuse component in
the STFT domain. Performance for different values of $`D`$ is shown in
Fig.
[6](#S5.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ V-A1 RTF-MCLP Algorithm Parameters ‣ V-A Stationary source, batch processing ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")(d-f).
Again there is a peak performance for $`D=1`$ and $`D=2`$. $`D=0`$ case
uses immediate past value for prediction, which results in degradation
of the estimated signal due to the high correlation between successive
STFT frames. Higher values of $`D`$ retains more of the diffuse
component in the desired signal, hence the degradation in performance
compared to the clean signal. Also, for higher $`D`$, the RTF
approximation does not hold good resulting in performance degradation.
Yet the performance is found to be better than using only MCLP in all
the cases.

#### V-A2 RIR conditions

RIR is a function of the distance and angular position of the source
with respect to the microphones, and $`RT60`$ value of the enclosure.
These parameters are studied individually by fixing the other two
parameters. The source distance and the angular position are varied as
shown in Fig.
[3](#S5.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")
(dotted line and circle in green), and the RT60 is varied from $`0.3~s`$
to $`1.2~s`$. The baseline values for the parameters are {source
distance$`=1.0~m`$, source angle$`=90^{o}`$, $`RT60=0.6~s`$}. The
algorithm parameters are fixed as {max iterations$`=5`$, $`L=12`$,
$`M=4`$, $`D=2`$}.

Fig.
[7](#S5.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ V-A2 RIR conditions ‣ V-A Stationary source, batch processing ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")
shows the performance comparison for different RIR conditions. We can
see that, (i) spatial filtering aids MCLP and hence improves the
dereverberation performance of MCLP method, (ii) joint spatial filtering
and MCLP based dereverberation in RTF-MCLP is slightly better compared
to the cascaded approach of MCLP dereverberation followed by spatial
filtering in C-RTF-MCLP, (iii) STOI value is more than $`0.9`$ for all
the acoustic conditions in all three MCLP methods indicating good
intelligibility of enhanced speech, and (iv) SDB performance is poor
compared to the MCLP based methods. Although all techniques deteriorate
with increasing $`RT60`$, the advantage of RTF-MCLP method is higher for
higher $`RT60`$ than MCLP (Fig.
[7](#S5.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ V-A2 RIR conditions ‣ V-A Stationary source, batch processing ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")(a-c)).
We see that the good performance of RTF-MCLP is over an RT60 range upto
$`0.7~s`$. The performance as a function of source distance, shown in
[7](#S5.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ V-A2 RIR conditions ‣ V-A Stationary source, batch processing ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")(d-f),
decreases approximately linearly with increasing distance. Increasing
the source distance decreases the SRR (signal to reverberation ratio),
which can be akin to increasing $`RT60`$. In terms of STOI, a source
distance of $`2.5~m`$ has a similar effect as $`RT60=1.2~s`$. The
angular performance plots in
[7](#S5.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ V-A2 RIR conditions ‣ V-A Stationary source, batch processing ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")(g-i)
show that the improvement is approximately uniform for all angular
positions of the source, because of the omni-directional microphones
assumed.

#### V-A3 Directional speech interference

Next, we study the performance of the RTF-MCLP method in the presence of
an interfering speech source, with $`0~dB`$ signal to interference ratio
(SIR), at $`45^{o}`$ angular position. For this experiment we assume the
RTF vector of the desired speech source to be known a-priori. It is
computed using the discrete Fourier transform of the initial $`8~ms`$
after the direct component of the desired source RIR. Fig.
[8](#S5.F8 "Fig. 8 ‣ V-A3 Directional speech interference ‣ V-A Stationary source, batch processing ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")
shows the performance measures FwSNR, residual energy of the interferer
(IE) in dB, PESQ and STOI, as a function of the distance of the
interferer from the center of the array. The quantum of residual
inference at the output is determined by passing the known interference
signal through the MCLP and MVDR filters estimated using the mixture
microphone signal. At a $`0.5~m`$ distance, the interferer is near to
the array than the source and also to the reference microphone at
$`0^{o}`$ (the source is at $`1~m`$ distance and $`90^{o}`$ angular
position). In Fig.
[8](#S5.F8 "Fig. 8 ‣ V-A3 Directional speech interference ‣ V-A Stationary source, batch processing ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source"),
we can see that (i) MCLP performance gets severely degraded in the
presence of interference, (ii) the super directive beamformer
performance is better than MCLP for nearer source positions, i.e., when
the direct component is stronger than the reverb components, (iii)
cascaded MVDR beamformer at the output of the MCLP filter (C-RTF-MCLP)
improves the performance by $`3-4~dB`$ compared to the beamformer or the
MCLP filter alone, (iv) the new RTF-MCLP scheme further improves by
about $`1~dB`$. The PESQ performance is poor for all techniques, but
intelligibility is good in terms of STOI, close to $`0.9`$. The
interferer suppression is found to be slightly better in the C-RTF-MCLP
approach.

![Refer to caption](1910.09782v1/dirSpeech.png)

Fig. 8: Dereverberation performance for interfering speech source at
$`45^{o}`$.

### V-B Dynamic source dereverberation

We consider the experimental scenario shown in Fig.
[3](#S5.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")(b).
Both the adaptation parameters $`\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}`$ are fixed at
$`0.1`$, and $`\epsilon=10^{-6}`$. We evaluate the signal estimation
performance using segment-wise FwSNR measure. The restoration of short
time spectrum is quantified by the segment-wise LLR measure. The segment
measures shown are computed every $`10~ms`$ with $`25~ms`$ windows and
smoothed using triangular window with $`1~s`$ ($`100`$ segments)
temporal context. We compare results of the online RTF-MCLP approach to
the Kalman filter method of \[[31](#bib.bib31)\]. Time-varying MCLP in
the RTF-MCLP method is different from \[[31](#bib.bib31)\] in the
following assumptions: in \[[31](#bib.bib31)\], (i) the desired signal
spatial covariance matrix is full rank
$`{\bf d}[n,k]\sim\mathcal{N}_{c}\left({\bf 0},\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{d}[n,k]\right)`$,
and (ii) the distribution of $`{\bf i}_{m,n}[k]`$ is an isotropic
Gaussian, identically distributed for each $`m`$,
$`{\bf g}_{m,n}[k]\sim\mathcal{N}_{c}\left({\bf 0},\lambda{\bf I}\right)`$.
Because of assumption-(i), the Kalman filter approach requires
computation of a matrix inverse for each STFT index $`n,k`$, hence
computationally more expensive. Average per frame computation time on a
laptop with Intel (R) Core(TM) i5-4210U CPU @ 1.7 GHz processor is found
to be $`1.07~sec`$ and $`0.18~sec`$ for the Kalman filter approach and
the RTF-MCLP respectively providing a ten-fold reduction. We examine
three experimental scenarios in the following, single source with
position change, two simultaneous sources and a moving source. Two BBC
news clips of duration $`\approx 18~s`$ are used as test signals.

#### V-B1 Single source with position switch

In this experiment, we consider the source to switch from position-A to
position-B in Fig.
[3](#S5.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")
at $`18.6~s`$. This example is to test the adaptation of the online
RTF-MCLP to the switched source position. The objective performance
measures are shown in Fig.
[9](#S5.F9 "Fig. 9 ‣ V-B1 Single source with position switch ‣ V-B Dynamic source dereverberation ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source").
We see that, the performance of RTF-MCLP is better in-terms of both LLR
and FwSNR measures than the Kalman filter approach, during the
steady-state portions. But, the performance does degrade at the source
change point (transient response). It is found to be slightly poorer
than the Kalman filter approach, probably due to the choice of
parameters $`\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\epsilon\}`$, which result in a
trade-off between the transient and steady-state performances.

![Refer to caption](1910.09782v1/plots_SPC.png)

Fig. 9: LLR and FwSNR measures for the source position change scenario.

#### V-B2 Stationary, two simultaneous sources

The performance of estimating a desired source in a two source scenario
is shown in Fig.
[10](#S5.F10 "Fig. 10 ‣ V-B2 Stationary, two simultaneous sources ‣ V-B Dynamic source dereverberation ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source").
Two different BBC news clips are played simultaneously with equal
strength ($`0~dB`$ signal to interference ratio) from positions A and B,
shown in Fig.
[3](#S5.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")(b).
The source at position-A is considered as the desired source. RTF
estimated from the first $`8~ms`$ (after direct path) of the RIR is
specified for the RTF-MCLP(k) method (i.e., RTF of desired source is
known a-priori). The objective performance measures in Fig.
[10](#S5.F10 "Fig. 10 ‣ V-B2 Stationary, two simultaneous sources ‣ V-B Dynamic source dereverberation ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")
show that, the MCLP based methods are effective even in multi source
scenario. The performance of RTF-MCLP is similar to the Kalman filter
approach, and shows improvement compared to reverberant speech. The
prior fixing of RTF in RTF-MCLP(k) improves the desired signal
estimation by $`\approx~5~dB`$, which can be seen distinctly in the
suppression of interference signal energy, FwSNR, and also LLR
improvement.

![Refer to caption](1910.09782v1/plots_TSS.png)

Fig. 10: LLR, FwSNR, and interference energy measures for two
simultaneous sources case; RTF-MCLP(k) shows results for the case with
RTF of the desired source known a-priori.

#### V-B3 Moving source

We consider a single source moving from position-D to position-C in Fig.
[3](#S5.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")(b)
along a linear path ($`2.5~m`$ distance) with a fixed speed in $`18~s`$.
The moving source recording is simulated by convolving the source signal
with the RIR changing every $`5~ms`$ (for the chosen positions and
duration, this corresponds to $`\approx 0.7~mm`$ separation between
successive positions). For dereverberation, the constants
$`\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}`$ are set to $`0.01`$, instead of $`0.1`$ as in
earlier fixed source position case. The results in Fig.
[11](#S5.F11 "Fig. 11 ‣ V-B3 Moving source ‣ V-B Dynamic source dereverberation ‣ V Experiments and Results ‣ Joint spatial filter and time-varying MCLP for dereverberation and interference suppression of a dynamic/static speech source")
show that time-varying MCLP is effective for moving source case as well,
and the RTF-MCLP method is better than the Kalman filter approach in
terms of both FwSNR and LLR measures. As the distance of source to
reference microphone is decreasing with time, we can see that FwSNR
improves with time, in both the methods. However, the performance
improvement over Kalman filter is less for the moving source case
compared to the stationary source cases discussed in the previous
section.

![Refer to caption](1910.09782v1/plot_online.png)

Fig. 11: LLR, and FwSNR measures for moving source experiment.

## VI Conclusions

Joint spatial filtering and multi channel linear prediction in the STFT
domain is developed for dereverberation of static or dynamic speech
sources in a single source and multiple source applications. For a
static source case, batch estimation is considered assuming stochastic
time-independence of speech STFT coefficients. The joint formulation of
spatial filtering and MCLP is found to provide effective
dereverberation, as well as interference suppression with minimum prior
knowledge of the source RTF. The extension of the joint formulation to
the moving source case is found to be equally effective because of
online spatial filtering and a linear dynamic system model for the MCLP.
The interferer suppression is good even at $`0~dB`$ SIR for a
directional separation of $`45^{o}`$.
